title: Is this change handling appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether issues and changes in a scenario are handled at the right level, by the right people, with the right technique, and pick the reason that explains it.
question: Draycott's product owner adds a new Must have feature that is not in the project backlog and trades out a Should have to make room. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?

teach.h: Four tests for any change decision
teach.body: Test a change decision four ways. Line: does it alter the project backlog? If so it is a baseline change and goes formal; if not, it is detail. Authority: is the right person deciding, the board or delegated change authority for baseline changes, the team with the product owner for detail? Technique: trading to absorb change, swarming for blockers. Escalation and record: issue to the PM only if the team cannot resolve it, formal issues in the issue register with an issue report.

teach.body: Two failures recur. Under-control: baseline changes slip in through trading or a product owner's say-so, and the board loses control of what the project delivers. Over-control: every small wording tweak is sent to the board, freezing the change that agile delivery should embrace. The issues practice sits between: welcome detail change at team level, and make formal decisions where the project backlog moves.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Callowmere's Student Support Hub
teach.body: The academic registrar wants the early-warning feature added to Release 1, which would change the project backlog and the agreed release map. Project manager Jamal Hussain logs a request for change and writes an issue report covering the Welcome Week date, the ethics committee review and options, for the board to decide. When wellbeing staff ask for clearer wording on a confirmation screen, product owner Rebecca Lyle agrees it with the team as a detail change. When Northmere's test link fails, the web team swarms first, then escalates to Jamal.

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: Choose the one that explains this case

teach.text: Traps: 'the PO owns the product backlog' is true but gives no authority over the project baseline. 'Trading keeps the workload balanced' is true but does not make a new epic a detail change. 'All formal issues go in the issue register' is true but does not mean every small change must be formal. A blocker is an issue for the PM only after the team has tried to resolve it, and an exception only when a tolerance is at risk.

items: The project backlog is the line: changed means formal, unchanged means detail.
Baseline changes: project board or delegated change authority, with an issue report.
Detail changes: team level, priority agreed with the PO, often by trading.
Trade items of similar effort; swarm on blockers before escalating to the PM.
Watch for both under-control and over-control; agile welcomes change within control.

summary: You can now judge whether a scenario handles change at the right level, with the right decision maker, technique and escalation. You can also reject reasons that are true but do not explain why the handling fits or fails.

A.q: Draycott's maintenance engineers ask for a new feature that links alerts to the spare parts store, which they rate as a Must have. It is not in the project backlog. Product owner Leanne Park adds it to the software team's product backlog and trades out a Should have story of similar effort. How well does this apply the issues practice, and why?
options: Well, because trading keeps the workload balanced
Well, because the PO owns the team's product backlog
Poorly, because a baseline change needs a formal decision
Poorly, because trading needs the board's prior approval
A.why: A new Must have requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline; it needs formal handling and a decision by the board or delegated change authority (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Trading does keep workload level, but it is for changes within the project backlog, not new baseline items.
whyNot.1: The PO owns the product backlog, but that gives no authority to change the project baseline.
whyNot.3: Trading for detail changes is agreed at team level with the PO; the board's approval is not needed for those.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team hits a configuration fault in its test environment that stops two stories. Within an hour the product owner raises an exception report to the board, although no tolerance is forecast to be exceeded and the team has not yet looked at the fault together. What should have happened FIRST?
options: The PO should have traded the blocked stories away
The team should have swarmed on the blocker
The CPO should have updated the release map
The board should have reassessed the Agilometer
A.why: Swarming is the team's first response to a blocker; it escalates an issue to the PM only if it cannot resolve it, and an exception arises only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (11.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Trading absorbs changes in requirements; it does not clear a blocker.
whyNot.2: A short-lived blocker does not call for release map changes, and the CPO does not handle team blockers.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer assesses agile-working risk; it does not resolve a technical blocker.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's issue management approach says that every change to the app, however small, needs a written request for change approved by the project board before the team may act. How well does this suit the project's agile delivery, and why?
options: Well, because the board keeps control of all the scope
Well, because Coinbridge's contract needs formal variations
Poorly, because the CPO decides every change to the app
Poorly, because detail changes are handled at team level
A.why: Changes that do not affect the project backlog are detail changes handled informally at team level; agile delivery should embrace and support change (11.3.2, Table 11.1).

whyNot.0: The board controls the baseline; sending every small change to it freezes the change agile should welcome.
whyNot.1: Coinbridge's scope changes may need variations, but that does not justify formal handling for every change to the app.
whyNot.2: The CPO prioritizes across teams; detail changes are agreed at team level with the PO, and baseline changes go to the board or change authority.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's project board has delegated authority for baseline changes below £20,000 to Dr Rajesh Iyer, the principal social worker. A new Must have epic for an easy-read version of the self-assessment would cost £12,000 and change the project backlog. Who should decide whether it goes ahead?
options: The digital team's product owner
Simon Archer, the project manager
Dr Rajesh Iyer, the change authority
Gita Bhatt, the incoming agile coach
B.why: Baseline changes are decided by the project board or by the person or persons given delegated authority to decide on changes (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: The PO agrees detail changes at team level; this change alters the project backlog.
whyNot.1: The PM captures and assesses the issue, but the delegated authority to decide lies with Dr Iyer.
whyNot.3: The agile coach supports agile adoption; she has no authority over baseline changes.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team wants to bring a new 13-point story into the current iteration. With its product owner's agreement, the team makes room by removing a 2-point story. What is the MAIN flaw in this trade?
options: Trades need the project board's approval
New stories must wait for the next stage
The swap should be raised as an exception
The items swapped are not of similar effort
B.why: Successful trading swaps items of similar effort, with priorities agreed with the PO, so scope and the iteration stay balanced (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Trading within the project backlog is a team-level decision with the PO, not a board decision.
whyNot.1: Agile embraces change; detail changes can be absorbed within the iteration by trading.
whyNot.2: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; the flaw is the uneven swap.

B.q: Callowmere University's students' union asks for a new live chat feature with counsellors as a Must have for Release 1. It is not in the project backlog. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Add it to the web team's next sprint backlog
Ask the web team to swarm on it
Record it as a new threat in the risk register
Capture it as a request for change and assess it
B.why: A new Must have requirement that would change the project backlog is a request for change to the baseline; it is captured and assessed for formal decision (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Adding a new baseline item to a sprint bypasses the formal decision it needs.
whyNot.1: Swarming is for blockers or urgent work, not for deciding whether to accept new scope.
whyNot.2: The request has already been made, so it is an issue, not an uncertain future event.

C.q: Callowmere University's academic registrar insists that the early-warning feature, pencilled in as a possible Release 3 item, be added to Release 1, which would change the project backlog. Project manager Jamal Hussain logs it as a request for change and writes an issue report setting out the impact on the Welcome Week date, the ethics committee's review, the options and his recommendation for the board. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a baseline change is assessed and decided formally
Yes, because the registrar is a senior university stakeholder
No, because the product owner should trade it into Release 1
No, because a new feature should go in an exception report
C.why: A change to the agreed baseline needs formal handling: the issue report describes impacts on the baseline, options and a recommendation for the board or change authority (11.3.2, 11.3.4).

whyNot.1: The registrar's seniority is true but does not explain why formal handling is right.
whyNot.2: Trading is for changes within the project backlog; this request changes the project backlog itself.
whyNot.3: An exception report is for a forecast breach of tolerance, not for assessing a request for change.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's tenants' panel asks for a larger font on one page of the tenant portal. The change does not affect the project backlog. Project manager Sally Greaves raises a request for change with a full issue report for the board, and the change waits three weeks for the next board meeting. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because all issues are recorded in the issue register
Yes, because the board includes tenant members
No, because a detail change is handled at team level
No, because it should be raised as an exception
C.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level; agile should embrace such change rather than delay it (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Formal issues are recorded in the register, but this change does not need formal handling.
whyNot.1: Tenant members on the board are true of the scenario but irrelevant to how a detail change is handled.
whyNot.3: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so an exception does not apply.

C.q: During a sprint, Pinewick's e-commerce team learns that customers need a 'ready to collect' text message, a story within an existing epic. Product owner Anita Shah agrees its priority with the team, and they remove a lower-priority story of similar effort so the sprint stays on track. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board has fixed the date and the budget
Yes, because similar-effort items were swapped with the PO
No, because trading should be decided by the project board
No, because new stories should be swarmed on instead
C.why: Trading replaces requirements with others of similar effort, with priorities agreed with the PO, absorbing a detail change without growing scope (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Fixed time and cost are true of the project but do not explain why this trade is the right handling.
whyNot.2: Detail changes within the project backlog are handled at team level with the PO, not by the board.
whyNot.3: Swarming is for blockers or urgent items; absorbing a new requirement is what trading is for.

reteach.title: A building's refit
reteach.question: A school's hall is being refitted to an agreed design and budget. Which changes can the site team agree on the spot, and which go back to the governors?

blocks.body: Moving a light switch a few centimetres, or swapping one paint colour for another at the same price, is detail: the site manager and the head teacher agree it. Adding a stage that was never in the design changes what was agreed, so the governors decide, with a short report on cost, time and options. Sending every paint choice to the governors would stall the work; letting the site team add a stage would take away the governors' control.

blocks.text: A site manager's enthusiasm for the stage does not change who decides. If the agreed design changes, the governors decide.

explain.body: Does the change alter the project backlog? If yes, it is a baseline change and goes formal. If no, it is detail, handled informally by the team.

test.q: Easterholm's digital team receives two requests. One adds a new Must have epic for video call assessments that is not in the project backlog; the other clarifies a question's wording within an existing story. How should they be handled?
options: Both formally, through the project board
Both at team level, by the product owner
The wording formally; the new epic at team level
The new epic formally; the wording at team level
test.why: A change that alters the project backlog is a baseline change handled formally; one that does not is a detail change handled at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: The wording change does not affect the project backlog, so it does not need formal handling.
whyNot.1: The new epic changes the project backlog, so it needs a formal decision.
whyNot.2: This reverses the rule: the epic changes the baseline and the wording does not.

explain.body: Baseline changes are decided by the project board or by whoever it has given delegated change authority. Detail changes are agreed at team level with the product owner.

test.q: Draycott's board has made Ruth Kenyon, the head of maintenance, the change authority for baseline changes within stage tolerances. A request to add Factory A's air compressors to Release 2 as a Must have would change the project backlog and is within tolerance. The software team lead approves it herself. What is the flaw?
options: It should have been traded at team level
It should have gone to Ruth Kenyon to decide
It should have been raised as an exception
It should have been added to the risk register
test.why: Baseline changes are decided by the board or by the person given delegated change authority, here Ruth Kenyon (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Trading is for detail changes; this one alters the project backlog.
whyNot.2: The change is within tolerance, so it is not an exception.
whyNot.3: The request is an issue to be decided, not an uncertain future event.

explain.body: Trading absorbs new or changed requirements by swapping items of similar effort, agreed with the PO. Swarming clears a blocker by putting the whole team on it.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's app team is asked to add a detail to the claim screen within an existing story. The team proposes to swarm on the new detail so it can be finished this sprint, without removing anything. What is the BEST criticism?
options: Swarming should be used for blockers, not for scope
The board should have approved the swarm first
The new detail should be raised as an exception
Detail changes should wait for the next release
test.why: Absorbing new requirements is done by trading items of similar effort with the PO; swarming is for blockers or time-critical work (11.4.1, 11.4.2).

whyNot.1: The board does not approve team techniques such as swarming.
whyNot.2: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so this is not an exception.
whyNot.3: Agile embraces detail change within the iteration through trading.

explain.body: A blocker the team cannot clear goes to the PM as an issue. Formal issues are logged in the issue register, with an issue report for the decision. An exception arises only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

items.label: exception if tolerance is at risk

test.q: Pinewick's store operations team has swarmed on a stock system fault for two days and cannot fix it, because the fix lies with Tallis. No tolerance is yet forecast to be exceeded. Sophie Draper escalates it to the project manager, who logs it in the issue register. How well does this apply the issues practice?
options: Well, as the team escalated after trying to resolve it
Well, as every blocker is decided by the project board
Poorly, as it should go to the board as an exception
Poorly, as the team should keep swarming until fixed
test.why: If swarming cannot resolve a blocker, the team escalates it to the PM as an issue; an exception arises only if tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (11.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.1: The PM handles escalated issues; the board decides baseline changes and exceptions, not every blocker.
whyNot.2: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so an exception report is not yet needed.
whyNot.3: The cause lies with Tallis, outside the team's control, so escalating to the PM is right.
